n: In contrast to Barnabas, a couple named Ananias and Sapphira also sell some property.

f.g: Hebrew Hananiah, “the Lord is gracious” — an ironic name given the story.
The word links this story to Barnabas’s generous gift in Acts 4:36-37.

n: With his wife’s full knowledge, Ananias secretly keeps part of the money and presents the rest as if it were the whole amount. Their sin is not keeping money but pretending.

f.g: The same rare Greek verb describes Achan’s theft of devoted things in Joshua 7:1 (Greek Old Testament).
privy = secretly aware of, in on it.

n: Peter, discerning by the Spirit, asks why Ananias let Satan fill his heart to lie to the Holy Ghost by holding back part of the price.

f.w: to lie to the Holy Ghost

n: The land was his to keep, and the money was his to use. Giving was voluntary. His real offense was deception — lying not to men but to God. Note that lying to the Holy Ghost is called lying to God.

f.g: Consecration in the early Church was freely chosen, not forced.

f.w: thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God

n: Hearing this, Ananias collapses and dies. Great fear grips everyone who hears about it.

f.g: died.
Deep reverence and awe for the holiness of God.

n: Young men wrap the body and carry him out for burial. Burial typically took place the same day in that climate.

f.g: Wrapped the body in cloth for burial.

n: About three hours later his wife comes in, unaware of what has happened.

f.g: space = period of time.

n: Peter gives her a chance to tell the truth, asking if they sold the land for this amount. She says yes — repeating the lie.

f.w: Tell me whether ye sold the land for so much?
f.g: Peter’s question offers her an opportunity to be honest.

n: Peter asks how they could agree together to test the Spirit of the Lord. The men who buried her husband are at the door and will carry her out too.

f.w: tempt the Spirit of the Lord
f.g: tempt = put to the test, see how much one can get away with.

n: She falls at his feet and dies, and the young men bury her beside her husband.

f.g: died.

n: Great fear comes on the whole church and all who hear. This is Luke’s first use of the word “church” — a community set apart as holy, where God is not mocked.

f.g: Greek ekklēsia — an assembly “called out,” used in the Greek Old Testament for Israel’s congregation.

n: The apostles perform many signs and wonders among the people, and the believers regularly gather together in Solomon’s Porch at the temple.
Outsiders don’t dare join them casually, though the people hold them in high esteem.

f.g: durst = dared.
magnified = praised, held in high regard.

n: Still, more and more believers — crowds of men and women — are added to the Lord.

f.w: multitudes both of men and women

n: People carry the sick into the streets on cots and mats, hoping even Peter’s shadow might fall on some of them as he passes.
Crowds also come from towns around Jerusalem bringing the sick and those troubled by evil spirits, and all are healed.

f.g: vexed = tormented.

n: The high priest and his Sadducee allies are filled with jealousy.

f.g: Greek zēlos — jealousy, envy.

n: They arrest the apostles and put them in the public jail.

f.g: The public jail.

n: But during the night an angel of the Lord opens the prison doors and leads them out.
The angel commands them to go stand in the temple and tell the people the full message of this new life.

f.w: all the words of this life

n: At dawn they are teaching in the temple. Meanwhile the high priest convenes the full Sanhedrin and the council of elders, and sends for the prisoners.

f.w: all the senate of the children of Israel
f.g: The full body of Israel’s elders.

n: The officers come back without them.

f.w: found them not in the prison
f.g: A touch of humor in Luke’s storytelling.

n: They report that the jail was securely locked and the guards were at their posts — but no one was inside.

f.w: the keepers standing without before the doors
f.g: keepers = guards; without = outside.

n: The leaders are baffled, wondering where this will lead.

f.w: they doubted of them whereunto this would grow
f.g: They were perplexed about what this would come to.

n: Then someone reports that the men they jailed are standing in the temple, teaching the people.

f.w: standing in the temple, and teaching

n: The captain and officers bring them in without force, fearing the crowd might stone them.

f.g: The leaders feared the people more than the apostles feared the leaders.

n: They stand the apostles before the council for questioning by the high priest.

He reminds them of the strict order not to teach in “this name” — refusing even to say Jesus’s name — and accuses them of filling Jerusalem with their teaching and blaming the leaders for Jesus’s death.

f.w: bring this man's blood upon us

f.g: straitly = strictly.

n: Peter and the apostles give a clear principle: we must obey God rather than men.

f.w: We ought to obey God rather than men

n: The God of their ancestors raised up Jesus, whom the leaders killed by hanging him on a tree — a phrase recalling the law’s curse on one hanged on a tree.
God exalted him to his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give Israel repentance and forgiveness. Even repentance is a gift from Christ.
The apostles are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Ghost, whom God gives to those who obey him. Human and divine testimony stand together.

f.w: so is also the Holy Ghost

n: Enraged, the council wants to kill them.

f.g: Here, infuriated — the opposite reaction to the repentant crowd in Acts 2:37.

n: Gamaliel, a respected Pharisee and teacher of the law, stands up and asks that the apostles be sent out briefly.

f.g: A leading rabbi, grandson of the famous Hillel, and teacher of Saul of Tarsus.
doctor = teacher.

n: He urges caution: be careful what you do to these men.

f.g: take heed = be careful.

n: He cites Theudas, who claimed to be someone important and gathered about four hundred men, but was killed, and his movement collapsed.

f.g: Little is known of this Theudas; scholars debate his identity and date.
came to nothing.

n: Then Judas the Galilean rose up during the census, led a revolt, and also perished, his followers scattered.

f.g: Led a tax revolt around AD 6, against the Roman census under Quirinius.
the census for taxation.

n: His advice: leave these men alone. If this movement is merely human, it will fail on its own.
But if it is from God, they cannot stop it — and might even find themselves fighting God. Wise counsel, and true.

f.w: if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it

f.g: haply = perhaps, by chance.

n: The council agrees, but still has the apostles flogged, orders them not to speak in Jesus’s name, and releases them.

f.g: Probably the synagogue punishment of up to 39 lashes.

n: The apostles leave rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer disgrace for Jesus’s name.

f.w: rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name

n: Every day, in the temple and from house to house, they never stop teaching and proclaiming Jesus as the Christ.

f.w: they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ
